newsitem.title: USA: Hedge fund founder sees problems with mutual funds.
newsitem.headline: Hedge fund founder sees problems with mutual funds.

text.p: The recent explosion in growth among hedge funds has been due, in part, to increasing uneasieness over mutual funds, said one hedge fund manager.
The more than 2,000 hedge funds are still dwarfed by the number of mutual funds. But Michael DiCarlo, founder of DFS Advisors in Boston, said he believed the big growth would be in hedge funds.
"In Boston, there are more hedge fund managers than mutual fund managers," said DiCarlo said. "Mutual funds are being consolidated dramatically," he added. "That is going to continue."

DiCarlo, speaking at the Managed Account Reports' Mid-Year Conference on Alternative Investment Strategies here, noted that it was his dream to start his own company for much of the 18 years he was a fund manager at John Hancock Advisers.
"A lot of people want to own their own companies," he said later. "As (mutual fund) companies grow, people are saying, 'this is not the company I used to work for.'"
He echoed the thoughts of other portfolio managers in saying that it was becoming difficult to manage large funds with billions of dollars.

"Bigger is not necessarily better," DiCarlo said, adding that he started his hedge fund with $42 million in November and intends to keep it to a maximum of $200 million. He said he turned down $340 million in investments because he wanted to run his fund on his own terms.
Meanwhile, he said mutual funds have many more restrictions than hedge funds, such as the inability to short and buy derivatives. Hedge funds, he noted, are for the "sophisticated investor."
DiCarlo's funds are primarily equity oriented, but he said much of the latest runup in the stock market was due to falling interest rates, a trend he expected to continue.

"In 18 to 24 months, I wouldn't be surprised to see the (U.S. Treasury 30-year) long bond approaching 5 percent," he said. "We think inflation is going down. "Wages are up but modestly and benefits are down, so total compensation is down," DiCarlo said.
"I am bullish," he said, "to extremely bullish."
